I often lose total motivation to program and was just wondering if people could share some tips on how they do it.
How can I get the motivation to complete my game?

I could really use advice here too, my main thing is always force myself to do a bit each night, but inevitably I break this chain and take a few weeks to get on track again. I think my main problem is I always try to do it as a solo endeavor. I often feel like if I had an artist as equally motivated about the game as me, I could stay more on track as I would know someone is counting on me.

You doing this totally alone or with some friends? Because the one thing that motivates me the most is a feeling of... debt, I guess, or at least responsibility... to the team of people who have also put their time and talent into this game that we're making.

Well, I don't have experience in making games per say, but I could give you some advice about personal motivation. When it comes to projects like these, it's best to approach it when a particularly good and exciting idea pops in your mind. It's like having a writers block when you don't have anything to spark yourself into finishing your game. Instead of trying to pound away at it consistently, take a break and do something else for a while. When an awesome idea hits you, don't hesitate. Just hop back on your project when it does and you'll find yourself completing your game and actually possibly making it better than what you intended.

Motivation is a fairly fluid and person specific thing. You could hear 50 different things from 50 different people on it and each one might apply. Or none of them. Here's mine, maybe it will apply:

For me, it's a matter of passion. If you are passionate about the project you're working on, you'll strive to finish it no matter what. I'm somewhere around 18 month into a project that I was once VERY passionate about. I kept a very demanding schedule and worked my ass off on it for an entire year. Then I got pretty sick and couldn't work on it for a while. It took time to heal and even longer to get the motivation back. I felt like I had lost my mojo, and the end was so far away and that it was just too hard to complete on my own. But I believed in the project and I found my stride again.

2 months later, a flood takes out my development PC. That, combined with a lax backup schedule (from being sick) caused me to lose about 6 weeks of work. I was basically back to where I was before I got sick. It was... extremely personally devastating. It had been a prolific 2 months of work, and I had sorted out a lot of problems with the game engine. I hit a couple of weeks of depression, picked myself up again and started back to work.

I got to about 2 weeks of work away from being back where I was before the flood hit, and my motivation just falls out completely. I'm just so frustrated because this game is going to take another 2 years to finish on my own. I believe in the project and I'm passionate about it, but it's been a special kind of struggle at this point.

A few weeks ago, I decided to take a break from it. I wanted to work on something much smaller for a while, finish that and come back to my big project with a fresh mind. So now, I'm making a small progen/RPG/survival project until I get the mojo back for the other one.

You may play my current progress demo if you want to: http://ttopgames.com/MicroRPG1.2/index.html

EDIT: Not sure if any of this helps. It's just my own personal struggle with finishing my game.

I have found that taking breaks from programming really helps. At the moment, I'm working on a game by myself. While this makes work much slower, it allows me to jump between different portions of the game. So if I get tired of programming (which I feel now), I'll do some art. When I get tired of art, I do some programming.

It may also help to start working on an entirely different project. However, this might be a slippery slope. You could end up abandoning your old project to start this new one. Then you may find yourself bored of the new project. As such, a terrible cycle starts.

find yourself some sheet metal and a couple springs. cut two circles from the sheet metal the size of the battery. If you have a hammer and a hard surface, pound them slightly convex and then solder your leads to the inside of the curve. attach (glue) this to one end of your box, with the leads sticking out. The muscles in your adomen are easiest to lose track of, meaning you can tense them up so hard that you get acid reflux or nausea. The shaking, high pulse, and sense of dread are all consistent with panic attacks.
